category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The hyoid bone is unique in the human skeleton because it does not [___] with any other bone.
back: * Articulate * It is held in place by muscles and ligaments * Provides a mobile anchor for the tongue and larynx

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A forensic examination of a suspected strangulation victim reveals a fracture of a U-shaped bone in the neck. This finding specifically targets the [___].
back: * Hyoid bone * Typically involves the greater cornua * Occurs due to inward compression against the cervical vertebrae

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Explain how the hyoid bone facilitates the movement of the tongue during the voluntary phase of deglutition.
back: * Acts as the base for the tongue * Provides attachment for the genioglossus and hyoglossus * Elevates to help the tongue push the bolus into the pharynx

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Contrast the embryological origins of the lesser cornua versus the greater cornua of the hyoid bone.
back: * Lesser Cornua: Derived from the 2nd pharyngeal arch (Reichert's cartilage) * Greater Cornua: Derived from the 3rd pharyngeal arch * Body: Formed by both 2nd and 3rd arch elements

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: List the four primary 'Suprahyoid' muscles that attach to and elevate the hyoid bone.
back: * Digastric (Anterior and Posterior bellies) * Mylohyoid * Stylohyoid * Geniohyoid

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The fibrous sheet connecting the superior border of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone is the [___].
back: * Thyrohyoid membrane * Pierced by the internal laryngeal nerve * Pierced by the superior laryngeal artery

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A 5-year-old child presents with a midline neck cyst that moves upward when the tongue is protruded. This occurs because the remnant duct is associated with the [___].
back: * Hyoid bone * Pathophysiology: Persistent thyroglossal duct * The duct often traverses or wraps around the hyoid body

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Detail the specific role of the infrahyoid muscles in the final phase of swallowing.
back: * Depress the hyoid bone * Pull the larynx downward to its resting position * Antagonize the suprahyoid muscles after bolus passage

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Contrast the attachments of the stylohyoid ligament with those of the stylomandibular ligament.
back: * Stylohyoid Ligament: Styloid process to the lesser cornu of hyoid * Stylomandibular Ligament: Styloid process to the angle of the mandible

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Name the three main anatomical parts that form the physical structure of the hyoid bone.
back: * Body (anterior part) * Greater Cornua (lateral projections) * Lesser Cornua (small superior projections)

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The hyoid bone is unique among the skeletal elements of the head and neck because it does not [___] with any other bone.
back:
* Articulate.
* It is suspended in the midline of the neck by muscles and ligaments.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A forensic autopsy of a 45-year-old male reveals a fractured hyoid bone. This finding is a classic diagnostic indicator for [___].
back:
* Manual strangulation.
* Hanging.
* Direct traumatic impact to the anterior neck.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Explain the role of the hyoid bone during the second (involuntary) stage of deglutition.
back:
* Acts as a mobile anchor.
* Suprahyoid muscles pull it superiorly/anteriorly.
* This elevation assists in closing the laryngeal inlet.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Contrast the skeletal connections of the greater cornu versus the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone.
back:
* Greater Cornu: Connects to the thyroid cartilage via the thyrohyoid membrane.
* Lesser Cornu: Connects to the styloid process via the stylohyoid ligament.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: List the three high-yield muscles that attach specifically to the greater cornu of the hyoid bone.
back:
* Middle constrictor of the pharynx.
* Hyoglossus muscle.
* Thyrohyoid muscle.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The fibrous or muscular band occasionally seen connecting a pyramidal lobe of the thyroid gland to the hyoid bone is the [___].
back:
* Levator glandulae thyroideae.
* It is an embryological remnant of the thyroglossal duct.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A patient presents with difficulty protruding the tongue. If the pathology involves the hyoid bone, which muscle attachment is likely compromised?
back:
* Genioglossus.
* It attaches to the body of the hyoid bone and the mental spines of the mandible.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Describe how the mylohyoid and geniohyoid muscles collaborate to influence the hyoid bone during oral processing.
back:
* Mylohyoid: Forms the floor of the mouth; elevates the hyoid.
* Geniohyoid: Pulls the hyoid bone anteriorly and superiorly.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Distinguish between the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscle groups based on their net effect on the hyoid bone's vertical position.
back:
* Suprahyoid: Elevates the hyoid bone (e.g., Digastric, Stylohyoid).
* Infrahyoid: Depresses the hyoid bone (e.g., Sternohyoid, Omohyoid).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Name the three anatomical parts that constitute the U-shaped framework of the hyoid bone.
back:
* Body (central portion).
* Greater cornua (projecting posteriorly).
* Lesser cornua (small superior projections).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Non-articulating nature of the Hyoid bone
front: The hyoid bone is unique in the human skeletal system because it does not [___] with any other bone.
back:
• Articulate.
• It is suspended in the midline by muscles and ligaments.
• Positioned at the level of the C3 vertebra.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A forensic pathologist finds a fractured hyoid bone during an autopsy of a patient with neck bruising. This finding is highly suggestive of [___].
back:
• Manual strangulation or throttling.
• Compression of the bone against the cervical vertebrae.
• High-yield forensic diagnostic marker.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Explain the role of the hyoid bone as a functional base for the tongue during movement.
back:
• Provides insertion for extrinsic tongue muscles (e.g., hyoglossus).
• Acts as an anchor for the floor of the mouth.
• Moves superiorly/anteriorly to facilitate bolus propulsion.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Contrast the attachments of the thyrohyoid membrane versus the stylohyoid ligament on the hyoid bone.
back:
• Thyrohyoid Membrane: Attaches to the upper border of the body and greater cornua.
• Stylohyoid Ligament: Attaches to the tip of the lesser cornua.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Identify the specific muscles that attach to the greater cornu of the hyoid bone.
back:
• Hyoglossus (tongue muscle).
• Middle constrictor of the pharynx.
• Thyrohyoid (infrahyoid).
• Stylohyoid (suprahyoid).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The [___] cornu of the hyoid bone is the primary attachment site for the stylohyoid ligament.
back:
• Lesser Cornu.
• Small conical projection at the junction of the body and greater cornu.
• Derived from the second pharyngeal arch.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: During neck surgery, a surgeon identifies a fibrous band connecting the pyramidal lobe of the thyroid to the hyoid body. Name this structure.
back:
• Levator glandulae thyroideae.
• A remnant of the thyroglossal duct.
• May be muscular or fibrous in nature.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Describe the mechanical action of the hyoid bone during the pharyngeal phase of deglutition.
back:
• Elevated by suprahyoid muscles.
• Pulls the larynx upward and forward.
• Helps in the closure of the laryngeal inlet by the epiglottis.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Distinguish between suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles based on their effect on hyoid position.
back:
• Suprahyoid: Elevate the hyoid bone (e.g., Mylohyoid, Digastric).
• Infrahyoid: Depress the hyoid bone (e.g., Sternohyoid, Omohyoid).
• Vital for swallowing and speech coordination.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: List the three primary anatomical components of the hyoid bone.
back:
• Body (central part).
• Greater Cornua (paired, lateral).
• Lesser Cornua (paired, superior).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The hyoid bone is described as a mobile, U-shaped bone that is unique because it [___] with any other bone in the body.
back: Does not articulate. It is suspended in the neck by muscles and ligaments from the skull, mandible, and larynx.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: During a forensic autopsy of a suspected strangulation victim, a fracture of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone is noted. This finding suggests [___].
back: Manual strangulation or hanging. Direct pressure on the neck forces the bone against the cervical vertebrae, leading to fracture.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Explain the role of the hyoid bone as a functional 'base' during the initial phase of swallowing.
back: Acts as an anchor for the tongue. Suprahyoid muscles contract to pull the hyoid and larynx superiorly and anteriorly, facilitating bolus passage.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Contrast the developmental origin and ligamentous attachment of the greater cornu versus the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone.
back: Greater Cornu: Derived from 3rd pharyngeal arch; attaches to thyrohyoid membrane. Lesser Cornu: Derived from 2nd arch; attaches to stylohyoid ligament.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Identify the specific infrahyoid muscle that attaches to the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage and the hyoid bone.
back: Thyrohyoid muscle. It functions to elevate the larynx toward the hyoid or depresses the hyoid bone toward the thyroid cartilage.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The [___] connects the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone to the styloid process of the temporal bone.
back: Stylohyoid ligament. This ligament occasionally ossifies, which may be visualized on lateral neck radiographs.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A patient presents with a midline neck swelling that moves upward when they protrude their tongue. This pathognomonic sign indicates a [___].
back: Thyroglossal cyst. It is a remnant of the thyroglossal duct, which often passes through or behind the hyoid bone.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: How does the hyoid bone maintain airway patency during deep inspiration or head extension?
back: Tension from suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles pulls the hyoid forward. This tethers the larynx and keeps the pharyngeal airway open.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Distinguish between the muscular attachments found on the body of the hyoid versus those on the greater cornu.
back: Body: Geniohyoid, Mylohyoid, Sternohyoid, Omohyoid. Greater Cornu: Hyoglossus, Middle constrictor, and Thyrohyoid.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: List the three main anatomical components that constitute the structure of the hyoid bone.
back: 1. Body (central). 2. Greater Cornua (paired, posterior). 3. Lesser Cornua (paired, superior).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The hyoid bone is unique among the skeletal structures of the neck because it does [___] with any other bone.
back:
• Not articulate
• Suspended by muscles and ligaments
• Located at C3 vertebral level

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: During a forensic autopsy of a suspected manual strangulation, a fracture of the U-shaped bone below the mandible is identified. Name this bone and its three primary parts.
back:
• Hyoid bone
• Central Body
• Pair of Greater Cornua (horns)
• Pair of Lesser Cornua

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Explain the ligamentous and membranous connections that suspend the hyoid bone between the skull and the larynx.
back:
• Stylohyoid ligaments: Connect lesser cornua to styloid processes
• Thyrohyoid membrane: Connects upper border to thyroid cartilage
• Hyo-epiglottic ligament: Connects body to epiglottis

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Contrast the role of the hyoid bone during the pharyngeal stage of deglutition versus its role in tongue protrusion.
back:
• Deglutition: Elevated by suprahyoids to lift the larynx, closing the airway
• Tongue Protrusion: Acts as a stable base for the Genioglossus muscle

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Identify the muscles specifically attaching to the lateral surface of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone.
back:
• Hyoglossus muscle (origin)
• Middle constrictor of the pharynx (origin)
• Thyrohyoid muscle (insertion)

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The [___] muscles attach to the hyoid bone from above to elevate it, whereas the [___] muscles attach from below to depress it.
back:
• Suprahyoid muscles (e.g., Digastric, Mylohyoid)
• Infrahyoid muscles (e.g., Sternohyoid, Omohyoid)
• Essential for speech and swallowing

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A 10-year-old presents with a midline neck mass below the hyoid bone that moves superiorly when the patient sticks out their tongue. Suggest the anatomical reason for this movement.
back:
• Thyroglossal cyst
• Remnant of the thyroglossal duct
• Duct is closely associated with or passes through the hyoid body

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Describe the specific functional attachment found at the tip of the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone.
back:
• Stylohyoid ligament
• Anchors the hyoid to the temporal bone
• Represents the ossified remnant of the second pharyngeal arch

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Compare the muscular attachments on the anterior surface of the hyoid body with those on the posterior surface.
back:
• Anterior: Geniohyoid, Mylohyoid, and Stylohyoid
• Posterior: None (Smooth surface related to thyrohyoid membrane and bursa)

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: List the two extrinsic tongue muscles that take their origin from the hyoid bone.
back:
• Hyoglossus (from greater cornu)
• Chondroglossus (from lesser cornu and body)

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The hyoid bone is uniquely characterized by its lack of articulation with any other bone; it is suspended from the styloid process of the temporal bone by the [___] ligament.
back: Stylohyoid ligament. • Connects the styloid process to the lesser cornu. • Occasionally undergoes ossification (Eagle syndrome).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A forensic examination of a 40-year-old male reveals a fractured hyoid bone and ecchymosis around the neck. This specific bony injury is most indicative of [___].
back: Manual strangulation or hanging. • Hyoid fracture is a classic forensic sign of neck compression. • Occurs due to the bone's proximity to the airway.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Explain the mechanical role of the hyoid bone during the pharyngeal phase of deglutition (swallowing).
back: • Serves as a mobile anchor for the tongue. • Suprahyoid muscles pull it upward and forward. • This elevation assists in closing the laryngeal inlet.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Contrast the attachments found on the greater cornua versus the lesser cornua of the hyoid bone.
back: • Greater Cornua: Attachments for Middle Pharyngeal Constrictor, Hyoglossus, and Thyrohyoid membrane. • Lesser Cornua: Attachments for Stylohyoid ligament and part of Middle Constrictor.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: List the vital neurovascular structures that pierce the thyrohyoid membrane, which connects the hyoid to the thyroid cartilage.
back: • Internal laryngeal nerve (sensory to upper larynx). • Superior laryngeal artery (branch of superior thyroid artery). • Essential for laryngeal sensation and blood supply.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A midline neck swelling that moves upward specifically during tongue protrusion is clinical evidence of a [___].
back: Thyroglossal duct cyst. • Caused by the persistent tract of thyroid descent. • The tract is closely associated with or loops around the hyoid bone.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A patient presents with inability to depress the hyoid bone after swallowing. Which specific group of muscles is likely dysfunctional?
back: Infrahyoid (Strap) muscles. • Includes Sternohyoid, Omohyoid, and Sternothyroid. • Primarily innervated by the Ansa Cervicalis (C1-C3).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Describe how the hyoid bone maintains airway patency during sleep and its relation to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA).
back: • Anchors the Genioglossus and Geniohyoid muscles. • Prevents the tongue from falling backward. • Surgical 'hyoid suspension' is used to treat severe OSA.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Contrast the innervation and action of the Mylohyoid versus the Geniohyoid muscles in relation to the hyoid bone.
back: • Mylohyoid: Nerve to Mylohyoid (V3); forms floor of mouth. • Geniohyoid: C1 fibers via Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); pulls hyoid anteriorly.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Identify the embryological origin of the different parts of the hyoid bone.
back: • Lesser Cornua and upper Body: Derived from 2nd Pharyngeal Arch (Reichert’s cartilage). • Greater Cornua and lower Body: Derived from 3rd Pharyngeal Arch.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Isolation of Hyoid bone in skeleton
front: The hyoid bone is uniquely characterized by its lack of [___] with any other bone in the human skeleton.
back:
• Articulation (or bony joint).
• It is suspended in the neck by muscles and ligaments.
• Serves as a mobile base for the tongue and a support for the larynx.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Clinical significance of hyoid fracture in forensics
front: A forensic pathologist examines a victim of suspected manual strangulation. Fracture of the [___] is a classic high-yield finding in this scenario.
back:
• Hyoid Bone (specifically the greater cornu).
• Indicates significant inward pressure on the neck.
• Often used as key evidence in suspected throttling or hanging cases.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Explain the role of the hyoid bone in facilitating the second stage (involuntary) of deglutition.
back:
• Suprahyoid muscles contract to elevate the hyoid.
• Elevation pulls the larynx upward and forward.
• This action helps the epiglottis seal the laryngeal inlet.
• Prevents food/liquid from entering the airway.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Pharyngeal arch derivatives of the hyoid
front: Contrast the embryological origins of the Greater Cornu and the Lesser Cornu of the hyoid bone.
back:
• Lesser Cornu: Derived from the Second Pharyngeal Arch (Reichert’s cartilage).
• Greater Cornu: Derived from the Third Pharyngeal Arch.
• The Body is split: upper part (2nd arch) and lower part (3rd arch).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Identify the extrinsic tongue muscle that originates from the superior border of the greater cornu of the hyoid.
back:
• Hyoglossus muscle.
• Action: Retracts and depresses the tongue.
• Innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
• Essential for stabilizing the tongue against the hyoid base.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The lesser cornu of the hyoid bone provides the site of attachment for the [___] ligament, connecting it to the temporal bone.
back:
• Stylohyoid ligament.
• Connects the styloid process to the lesser cornu.
• It is an embryological remnant of the second pharyngeal arch cartilage.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A patient presents with a midline neck swelling that moves upward during tongue protrusion. If this is a thyroglossal cyst, describe its relationship to the hyoid bone.
back:
• Cyst usually develops in the midline, often below the hyoid.
• The thyroglossal duct typically wraps around or traverses the hyoid body.
• Surgical excision (Sistrunk procedure) requires removing the central portion of the hyoid.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Describe how the hyoid bone's muscular stabilization contributes to the Valsalva maneuver during abdominal straining.
back:
• Infrahyoid muscles (Sternohyoid, Omohyoid) fix the bone downward.
• Provides a stable base for laryngeal muscles to close the rima glottidis.
• Prevents upward movement of the larynx while intrathoracic pressure is raised.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Distinguish between the muscle groups attached to the superior vs. inferior borders of the hyoid body.
back:
• Superior Border: Suprahyoid muscles (Geniohyoid, Mylohyoid, Genioglossus).
• Inferior Border: Infrahyoid muscles (Sternohyoid, Omohyoid, Thyrohyoid).
• Acts as the physical boundary between the floor of the mouth and the neck.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Specify the vertebral level corresponding to the resting anatomical position of the hyoid bone in the adult.
back:
• C3 (Third Cervical Vertebra).
• Located at the angle between the floor of the mouth and the upper neck.
• Serves as a reference point for the level of the epiglottis.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The hyoid bone is unique among skeletal elements in the human body because it does [___] with any other bone.
back: • Not articulate. • It is suspended in the midline of the neck by muscles and ligaments. • It serves as a mobile anchor for the tongue.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: In a forensic context, a 45-year-old male is found with a fractured hyoid bone and localized neck bruising. This finding is highly suggestive of [___].
back: • Manual strangulation or throttling. • The bone is susceptible to inward compression due to its isolated position in the neck.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: How does the hyoid bone facilitate the protection of the airway during the involuntary phase of deglutition?
back: • Suprahyoid muscles elevate the hyoid. • This elevation pulls the larynx upward and forward. • It helps the epiglottis seal the laryngeal inlet.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Contrast the skeletal and ligamentous attachments specific to the greater cornu versus the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone.
back: • Greater Cornu: Attaches the thyrohyoid membrane and middle constrictor muscle. • Lesser Cornu: Attaches the stylohyoid ligament (connecting to the styloid process).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Enlist the four suprahyoid muscles that attach to the hyoid bone to aid in its elevation.
back: • Digastric (anterior and posterior bellies). • Stylohyoid. • Mylohyoid. • Geniohyoid.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The [___] membrane connects the superior border of the thyroid cartilage to the posterior surface of the hyoid body and greater cornua.
back: • Thyrohyoid membrane. • It is pierced by the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A 10-year-old child presents with a midline neck mass that moves upward during tongue protrusion. This movement occurs because the mass is linked to the [___].
back: • Hyoid bone. • This occurs via remnants of the thyroglossal duct, which typically hooks around the hyoid during descent.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Explain the biological importance of the hyoid bone being suspended solely by soft tissue rather than fixed joints.
back: • Allows high mobility for vocalization and swallowing. • Permits the pharynx to expand during bolus passage. • Provides a dynamic platform for the tongue base.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Distinguish between the actions of the infrahyoid muscles and suprahyoid muscles on the hyoid bone.
back: • Suprahyoids: Elevate the hyoid bone and larynx. • Infrahyoids: Depress the hyoid bone and larynx (e.g., Sternohyoid, Omohyoid, Thyrohyoid).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Identify the three distinct anatomical components that form the U-shaped framework of the hyoid bone.
back: • Body (central portion). • Two Greater Cornua (lateral projections). • Two Lesser Cornua (small conical projections).

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Non-articulating nature of the Hyoid bone
front: The hyoid bone is unique in the human skeletal system because it [___] with any other bone.
back: * Does not articulate. * It is suspended in the neck by muscles and the stylohyoid ligament at the level of the C3 vertebra. * Serves as a mobile base for the tongue.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A victim of manual strangulation is found during forensic autopsy to have a fractured U-shaped bone in the midline of the neck. Identify the bone and its clinical relevance.
back: * Hyoid bone. * Fracture of this bone is a hallmark forensic indicator of strangulation or throttling. * Its mobility normally protects it from injury unless direct, sustained pressure is applied.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Functional role of Hyoid in swallowing
front: Describe the functional role of the hyoid bone during the process of deglutition (swallowing).
back: * Provides a mobile anchor for the tongue. * Suprahyoid muscles elevate the bone/larynx to seal the airway. * Infrahyoid muscles depress it to return the larynx to its resting position.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
coreConcept: Pharyngeal arch derivatives of Hyoid bone
front: Contrast the embryological derivatives of the lesser cornua and the greater cornua of the hyoid bone.
back: * Lesser cornua: Derived from the 2nd pharyngeal arch (Reichert’s cartilage). * Greater cornua: Derived from the 3rd pharyngeal arch. * The body is formed by both the 2nd and 3rd arches.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: List the three infrahyoid 'strap' muscles that attach directly to the hyoid bone and their primary function.
back: * Muscles: Sternohyoid, Omohyoid, and Thyrohyoid. * Function: These muscles depress the hyoid bone and larynx after elevation during swallowing and vocalization. * Innervation: Primarily by the Ansa Cervicalis.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The [___] connects the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone to the styloid process of the temporal bone, providing structural suspension.
back: * Stylohyoid ligament. * This ligament represents the remnant of the second pharyngeal arch. * Clinical Note: Excessive ossification can lead to Eagle Syndrome, causing throat pain and dysphagia.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A 10-year-old child presents with a midline neck mass that moves upward during tongue protrusion. Explain the anatomical relationship of this pathology to the hyoid bone.
back: * Thyroglossal cyst. * The thyroglossal duct descends from the tongue to the thyroid gland, often passing through or wrapping around the hyoid bone. * Protrusion pulls the duct and cyst superiorly.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Explain how the hyoid bone contributes to maintaining airway patency when a person is in the supine position.
back: * It provides attachment for the Genioglossus muscle. * Contraction of this muscle pulls the tongue forward. * This prevents the tongue from falling backward and obstructing the oropharynx.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Differentiate the skeletal attachments of the Mylohyoid and Geniohyoid muscles on the hyoid bone.
back: * Mylohyoid: Attaches to the anterior surface of the body. * Geniohyoid: Attaches to the superior surface of the body. * Both are suprahyoid muscles that elevate the bone during swallowing.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Identify the pharyngeal constrictor muscle that takes its origin from the greater and lesser cornua of the hyoid bone.
back: * Middle pharyngeal constrictor. * It is a fan-shaped muscle that overlaps the superior constrictor. * It helps propel the food bolus into the lower pharynx during the involuntary phase of deglutition.

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The hyoid bone is uniquely characterized by its lack of [___] with any other bone in the human skeleton.
back:
* Direct articulation
* Suspended by muscles and ligaments
* Connects to skull via stylohyoid ligament

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A forensic pathologist finds a fractured U-shaped bone between the mandible and larynx during an autopsy of a suspected murder victim. Identify the clinical implication.
back:
* Diagnosis: Fracture of the hyoid bone
* Significance: Strong indicator of manual strangulation or throttling
* Result: Compression against the cervical vertebrae

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Explain the role of the hyoid bone during the second stage of deglutition.
back:
* Acts as a mobile anchor for suprahyoid muscles
* Elevation pulls the larynx upward and forward
* Facilitates airway protection by closing the laryngeal inlet

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Contrast the attachments of the Thyrohyoid membrane versus the Thyrohyoid muscle on the hyoid bone.
back:
* Thyrohyoid Membrane: Attaches to the upper border of the body and greater cornua
* Thyrohyoid Muscle: Attaches to the lower border of the body and greater cornua

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Name the specific muscle that arises from the greater cornu and body of the hyoid to provide a base for the tongue.
back:
* Hyoglossus muscle
* Function: Depresses and retracts the tongue
* Innervation: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: The [___] ligament connects the lesser cornu of the hyoid bone to the styloid process of the temporal bone.
back:
* Stylohyoid ligament
* Represents part of the second pharyngeal arch
* May occasionally ossify

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: A pediatric patient presents with a midline neck cyst that moves superiorly when the tongue is protruded. Specify the bone typically involved in its surgical excision.
back:
* Diagnosis: Thyroglossal cyst
* Bone: Hyoid bone (central body)
* Procedure: Sistrunk procedure involves removing the central hyoid part

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Describe the coordinated action of the Mylohyoid and Geniohyoid muscles upon the hyoid bone.
back:
* Elevation of the hyoid bone and floor of mouth
* Pushes the food bolus backward into the pharynx
* Depresses the mandible when the hyoid is fixed

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: Distinguish between the greater cornua and the lesser cornua based on their structural morphology.
back:
* Greater Cornua: Long, flat processes projecting backward from the body
* Lesser Cornua: Small, conical eminences at the junction of the body and greater cornua

category: Describe the anatomical features of Hyoid bone and give attachments on the bone
front: List the three anatomical divisions that constitute the framework of the hyoid bone.
back:
* Body (central portion)
* Two Greater Cornua
* Two Lesser Cornua

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: The characteristic feature present in the transverse processes of all cervical vertebrae, used to transmit the vertebral artery in C1–C6, is the [___].
back:
• Foramen transversarium
• Located in the transverse process
• Transmits vertebral artery, veins, and sympathetic plexus (except C7)

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: A 25-year-old male presents with a neck injury after a diving accident. Imaging reveals a fracture of the dens (odontoid process). This structure is a unique identifying feature of [___].
back:
• Axis (C2 vertebra)
• The dens acts as a pivot for rotation
• Represents the developmentally fused body of C1

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Explain the anatomical mechanism of the 'No' movement (rotation) of the head.
back:
• Occurs at the atlanto-axial joints
• Pivot joint mechanism
• The Atlas (C1) rotates around the dens of the Axis (C2)

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Contrast the structural components of the Atlas (C1) with those of a typical cervical vertebra (C3-C6).
back:
• Atlas: No body or spinous process; consists of anterior/posterior arches and lateral masses.
• Typical: Small body, bifid spinous process, and foramen transversarium.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Identify the specific content of the foramen transversarium in the C7 vertebra and why it is unique.
back:
• Transmits vertebral veins only
• Does NOT transmit the vertebral artery
• The foramen is often smaller or absent compared to C1-C6

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: The spinous processes of typical cervical vertebrae (C3–C6) are uniquely [___] at their tips.
back:
• Bifid (split into two)
• Serves as attachment for the ligamentum nuchae and deep neck muscles

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: A patient presents with limited 'nodding' (Yes) movement of the head. Which specific articulation is likely involved?
back:
• Atlanto-occipital joint
• Between occipital condyles and superior articular facets of C1
• Functions as a synovial hinge joint

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Describe the functional significance of the transverse ligament of the atlas in maintaining spinal stability.
back:
• Holds the dens of C2 against the anterior arch of C1
• Prevents posterior displacement of the dens
• Crucial for protecting the spinal cord from compression

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Distinguish between the foramen transversarium and the vertebral foramen in cervical vertebrae.
back:
• Vertebral Foramen: Large and triangular; contains the spinal cord.
• Foramen Transversarium: Small hole in transverse process; contains vertebral vessels.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: List the three 'atypical' cervical vertebrae and their most prominent distinguishing feature.
back:
• C1 (Atlas): No body/spine
• C2 (Axis): Presence of Dens
• C7 (Vertebra Prominens): Long, non-bifid spinous process

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: The first cervical vertebra, known as the [___], is unique among all vertebrae because it lacks both a vertebral body and a spinous process.
back:
- Atlas (C1).
- Consists of anterior and posterior arches.
- Features lateral masses with facets for occipital condyles.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
coreConcept: Structure and Development of the Axis (C2)
front: A 25-year-old male involved in a high-speed motor vehicle accident presents with severe neck pain. Imaging reveals a fracture of the peg-like projection of C2. Identify the structure and its embryological origin.
back:
- Dens (Odontoid process).
- Represents the body of the Atlas (C1).
- Fuses with the body of the Axis (C2) during early development.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Describe the primary mechanical movement permitted by the atlanto-occipital joints and identify the articulating surfaces involved.
back:
- Nodding ('Yes') movement (flexion/extension).
- Occipital condyles of the skull.
- Superior articular facets of the Atlas (C1 lateral masses).

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
coreConcept: Atypical features of the C7 vertebra
front: Contrast a typical cervical vertebra (C3-C6) with the seventh cervical vertebra (C7) regarding their spinous processes and foramen transversarium contents.
back:
- Typical (C3-C6): Short, bifid spine; contains vertebral artery.
- C7 (Vertebra Prominens): Long, non-bifid spine; contains only vertebral veins.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
coreConcept: Vascular pathway of the Vertebral Artery
front: Identify the cervical level at which the vertebral artery typically first enters the foramen transversarium during its ascent to the brain.
back:
- C6 (Sixth cervical vertebra).
- It bypasses the foramen transversarium of C7.
- Ascends through C1 before entering the foramen magnum.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Most typical cervical vertebrae (C2–C6) are characterized by a [___] spinous process, providing attachment for the ligamentum nuchae and deep neck muscles.
back:
- Bifid (forked) spinous process.
- Increases surface area for muscle attachment.
- Absent in C1 and usually C7.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Cervical Spine
front: During a physical examination, a prominent bony landmark is palpated at the base of the neck during flexion. Identify the vertebra and the clinical significance of its transverse process.
back:
- C7 (Vertebra Prominens).
- Large transverse process.
- Foramen transversarium is small and does not transmit the vertebral artery.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
coreConcept: Functional Anatomy of the Atlanto-axial Joint
front: Explain how the transverse ligament of the atlas enables rotation of the head ('No' movement) at the atlanto-axial joint.
back:
- Binds the Dens of C2 to the anterior arch of C1.
- Forms a pivot joint (synovial).
- Allows C1 to rotate around the Dens as a fixed axis.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Distinguish between the superior articular surfaces of the Atlas (C1) and the Axis (C2) in terms of shape and function.
back:
- C1: Concave, kidney-shaped (cradle occipital condyles).
- C2: Large, flat, circular (allow gliding/rotation with C1).

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Enumerate the three primary 'atypical' cervical vertebrae and state one defining unique feature for each.
back:
- C1 (Atlas): No body or spine.
- C2 (Axis): Presence of the Dens.
- C7 (Prominens): Longest, non-bifid spinous process.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: The first cervical vertebra, known as the [___], is unique among all vertebrae because it completely lacks a vertebral body and a spinous process.
back:
• Atlas (C1).
• Consists of anterior and posterior arches.
• Features lateral masses with facets for occipital condyles (nodding joint).

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: A 25-year-old male sustains a 'Hangman’s fracture' following a high-velocity motor vehicle accident. The bony feature of the Axis that typically fractures or displaces in this injury is the [___].
back:
• Dens (Odontoid Process).
• Projects superiorly from the body of C2.
• Acts as a pivot for head rotation (atlanto-axial joint).

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Explain the specialized articulation of the Atlas (C1) that permits the 'Yes' (nodding) movement of the head.
back:
• Occurs at the Atlanto-occipital joints.
• Superior articular facets of C1 are concave/kidney-shaped.
• These articulate with convex occipital condyles of the skull.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Contrast C1 (Atlas) and C2 (Axis) regarding their primary structural differences and role in head movement.
back:
• C1: Ring-like, no body, no spine; allows flexion/extension (nodding).
• C2: Strongest cervical vertebra, has the Dens; allows rotation (shaking 'No').

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Identify the cervical vertebra termed the 'Vertebra Prominens' and list its two defining atypical features.
back:
• C7 vertebra.
• Longest spinous process (non-bifid).
• Foramen transversarium is small and does NOT transmit the vertebral artery.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Typical cervical vertebrae (C3–C6) are distinguished by having a [___] spinous process and a foramen transversarium.
back:
• Bifid (split in two).
• Foramen transversarium transmits the vertebral artery (except in C7).

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: A clinician palpates a prominent bony landmark at the base of the neck that does not disappear during neck flexion. Which specific vertebral part is being palpated?
back:
• Spinous process of C7 (Vertebra Prominens).
• It is thick, long, and nearly horizontal.
• Useful clinical landmark for counting vertebrae.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Describe the mechanical role of the Transverse Ligament of the Atlas during head rotation.
back:
• Connects the lateral masses of C1.
• Holds the Dens of C2 against the anterior arch of C1.
• Prevents the dens from damaging the spinal cord.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Distinguish typical cervical vertebrae from thoracic vertebrae based on the vertebral foramen and transverse processes.
back:
• Cervical: Large, triangular vertebral foramen; foramen transversarium present.
• Thoracic: Small, circular vertebral foramen; costal facets for ribs present.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Enumerate the two categories of cervical vertebrae and specify which levels belong to each.
back:
• Typical: C3, C4, C5, and C6.
• Atypical: C1 (Atlas), C2 (Axis), and C7 (Vertebra Prominens).

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: All cervical vertebrae are characterized by the presence of a hole in the transverse process called the [___].
back:
• Foramen transversarium
• Transmits the vertebral artery (C1–C6)
• Transmits vertebral veins and sympathetic nerves

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A 25-year-old male sustains a neck injury. Radiographs show a fracture of the peg-like projection of the C2 vertebra. Name this structure and its embryonic origin.
back:
• Dens (Odontoid process)
• Originates from the fused body of the Atlas (C1)
• Projects upward to articulate with the anterior arch of the Atlas

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Describe how the superior articular facets of the Atlas (C1) are specifically adapted for the atlanto-occipital joint.
back:
• Facets are kidney-shaped and deeply concave
• Articulate with convex occipital condyles
• Primary movement facilitated is the "nodding" (flexion/extension) of the head

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A patient presents with 'internal strabismus' and neck pain following a high-velocity trauma that ruptured the ligaments extending from the dens to the medial sides of the occipital condyles. Identify these ligaments and their function.
back:
• Alar ligaments
• Attach the dens to the foramen magnum
• Function to limit excessive rotation of the head

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: State the morphological differences of the spinous process in a typical cervical vertebra versus the seventh cervical vertebra.
back:
• Typical (C3–C6): Short and bifid (split)
• C7 (Vertebra Prominens): Very long, horizontal, and non-bifid
• C7 spine is easily palpable at the base of the neck

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: The primary structure preventing the dens from compromising the spinal cord by binding it to the anterior arch of the atlas is the [___].
back:
• Transverse ligament of the atlas
• Part of the cruciate (cruciform) ligament
• Attaches to the inner aspect of the lateral masses of C1

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A patient complains of pain when rotating their head. Anatomically, which cervical joint and specific bone feature allow the 'no' movement?
back:
• Atlanto-axial joint
• Pivot joint between the dens (C2) and anterior arch (C1)
• Rotation occurs around the vertical axis of the dens

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Explain the significance of the C7 foramen transversarium regarding its neurovascular contents compared to C1–C6.
back:
• C1–C6: Transmit both vertebral artery and vertebral veins
• C7: Transmits only the vertebral vein(s)
• The foramen in C7 is typically smaller and does not carry the artery

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Contrast the structural composition of the Atlas (C1) with a typical cervical vertebra (C3–C6).
back:
• Atlas: Lacks a vertebral body and a spinous process
• Consists of anterior and posterior arches and lateral masses
• Typical vertebra: Possesses a body, bifid spine, and pedicles/laminae

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: List the components of the 'triad' (Cruciate ligament) that stabilizes the C1-C2 complex.
back:
• Transverse ligament of the atlas (horizontal part)
• Superior vertical band (to foramen magnum)
• Inferior vertical band (to body of axis)

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: The distinguishing feature present in all cervical vertebrae, used to transmit the vertebral artery (except in C7) and sympathetic nerves, is the [___].
back:
• Foramen transversarium.
• Located within the transverse process.
• Transmits vertebral artery, veins, and sympathetic plexus.
• C7 foramen typically only transmits the accessory vertebral vein.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: A 25-year-old male is brought to the ER after a diving accident. Imaging shows a fracture of the pars interarticularis of the C2 vertebra. This specific clinical injury is known as [___].
back:
• Hangman's Fracture.
• Involves the Axis (C2).
• Usually caused by forceful hyperextension of the neck.
• Results in displacement of the C2 body anterior to C3.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Explain the role of the dens (odontoid process) and the transverse ligament during rotation of the head.
back:
• The dens of C2 acts as a pivot point.
• It articulates with the anterior arch of C1 (Atlas).
• The transverse ligament holds the dens in place.
• This allows the 'No' rotation movement of the head.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Contrast the T-tubule triad of skeletal muscle with the diad system of cardiac muscle.
back:
• Skeletal Triad: One T-tubule + two terminal cisternae at the A-I junction.
• Cardiac Diad: One T-tubule + one sarcoplasmic reticulum terminal at the Z-disc.
• Cardiac T-tubules are wider and less numerous.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: List the three atypical cervical vertebrae and provide the single most defining anatomical feature for each.
back:
• C1 (Atlas): No vertebral body or spinous process.
• C2 (Axis): Presence of the dens (odontoid process).
• C7 (Vertebra Prominens): Longest, non-bifid spinous process.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Unlike typical cervical vertebrae, the [___] vertebra has a spinous process that is long, thick, and not bifid.
back:
• Seventh Cervical Vertebra (C7).
• Known as the 'Vertebra Prominens'.
• Easily palpable at the base of the neck.
• Serves as a landmark for counting vertebrae.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: A patient presents with limited nodding ('Yes' movement) of the head. Which joint and anatomical features are primarily involved in this action?
back:
• Atlanto-occipital joint.
• Articulation: Occipital condyles + superior facets of C1 (Atlas).
• Facet Shape: Kidney-shaped and concave.
• Action: Flexion and extension of the head.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Compare the path of the vertebral artery in C1-C6 versus the C7 vertebra.
back:
• C1-C6: Vertebral artery passes through the foramen transversarium.
• C7: Foramen transversarium is small; transmits only the accessory vertebral vein.
• The vertebral artery enters the foramen at the C6 level.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Contrast the vertebral body and vertebral foramen shapes of cervical vertebrae with those of thoracic vertebrae.
back:
• Cervical: Small, kidney-shaped body; large, triangular vertebral foramen.
• Thoracic: Heart-shaped body; small, circular vertebral foramen.
• Cervical foramina are larger to accommodate the cervical spinal enlargement.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Define the 'Uncinate Processes' found in typical cervical vertebrae.
back:
• Upward projections on the lateral margins of C3-C7 bodies.
• Form uncovertebral joints (Joints of Luschka).
• Help stabilize the vertebral column and limit lateral flexion.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: The unique characteristic of cervical vertebrae is the presence of a [___] in each transverse process.
back:
● **Foramen transversarium**
● Transmits the vertebral artery (C1–C6)
● Transmits the vertebral vein (C1–C7)
● Located within the transverse process.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A 45-year-old male sustains a hyperextension injury to the neck. Imaging shows a fracture of the pedicles of C2. Identify this specific vertebra and its most prominent upward projection.
back:
● **Axis (C2)**
● **Dens (Odontoid Process)**: Projects upward from the body
● Represents the fused body of the Atlas (C1)
● Clinical: Involved in Hangman’s fracture.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Explain the functional role of the Cruciate ligament's transverse part at the atlanto-axial joint.
back:
● Binds the **dens** of C2 to the anterior arch of the atlas (C1)
● Prevents posterior displacement of the dens into the spinal cord
● Essential for stable rotation of the head.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Contrast the C7 vertebra (vertebra prominens) with a typical cervical vertebra regarding its spinous process and foramen transversarium contents.
back:
● **Spinous Process**: C7 is long and non-bifid; typical (C3-C6) are bifid
● **Contents**: C7 transmits only vertebral veins; typical transmit both vertebral artery and vein.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: List the specific bony attachments and primary function of the alar ligaments.
back:
● **Attachments**: Sides of the dens to the medial sides of occipital condyles
● **Function**: Limits excessive rotation of the head and atlas on the axis.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: The [___] vertebra is unique among cervical vertebrae because it lacks both a vertebral body and a spinous process.
back:
● **Atlas (C1)**
● Consists of anterior and posterior arches and two lateral masses
● Superior facets articulate with occipital condyles (Atlanto-occipital joint).

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A patient can nod 'Yes' (flexion/extension) but cannot shake their head 'No' (rotation). Identify the joints responsible for these specific movements.
back:
● **Nodding ('Yes')**: Atlanto-occipital joints
● **Rotation ('No')**: Atlanto-axial joints
● Rotation occurs around the dens of the axis.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Describe the mechanism and clinical significance of the uncovertebral joints (Joints of Luschka).
back:
● **Mechanism**: Synovial-like joints between uncinate processes of C3-C6 and the body above
● **Significance**: Common site for osteophyte formation leading to spinal nerve compression.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Contrast the anatomical orientation of superior articular facets in cervical versus thoracic vertebrae.
back:
● **Cervical**: Facets face upward and backward (oblique)
● **Thoracic**: Facets face backward and laterally (vertical)
● Cervical orientation permits high mobility in all planes.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Identify the palpable landmark of the C7 vertebra and the major ligamentous structure attaching to its tip.
back:
● **Landmark**: Long, non-bifid spinous process (Vertebra prominens)
● **Attachment**: Ligamentum nuchae
● Extends from the external occipital protuberance to C7.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: The distinguishing feature of a typical cervical vertebra that facilitates the passage of the vertebral artery is the [___].
back:
• Foramen transversarium
• Located within the transverse processes
• Transmits the vertebral artery (C1-C6) and vertebral veins

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A 25-year-old male presents after a high-velocity diving accident. Imaging reveals a 'Jefferson fracture'. This specific injury involves a burst fracture of which cervical vertebra?
back:
• C1 (Atlas)
• Characterized by fractures of the anterior and posterior arches
• Occurs due to vertical compression of the skull against the atlas

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Describe the anatomical mechanism that allows for the 'no' rotation of the head at the atlantoaxial joint.
back:
• Pivot-type synovial joint
• The atlas (C1) rotates around the dens (odontoid process) of the axis (C2)
• Rotation is limited by the alar ligaments

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A patient presents with severe neck pain following trauma. Contrast the structural composition of the C1 (atlas) and C2 (axis) vertebrae.
back:
• C1 (Atlas): Ring-like, lacks a body and spinous process; possesses lateral masses
• C2 (Axis): Possesses a dens (odontoid process) and the largest bifid spinous process

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Identify the clinical significance and primary muscle attachments of the C7 vertebra (vertebra prominens).
back:
• Feature: Longest, non-bifid spinous process used as a surface landmark
• Attachments: Ligamentum nuchae, Trapezius, Rhomboid minor, and Serratus posterior superior

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: The embryological equivalent of the body of the atlas (C1) which has fused with the body of the axis (C2) is the [___].
back:
• Dens (Odontoid process)
• Projects superiorly from the C2 body
• Serves as the axis of rotation for the atlas

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Following a motor vehicle accident, a patient experiences 'whiplash'. This clinical condition involves sudden hyperflexion and hyperextension, primarily stressing which ligament attached to the cervical spinous processes?
back:
• Ligamentum nuchae
• Extends from external occipital protuberance to C7 spine
• Limits excessive flexion of the cervical spine

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Explain the role of the transverse part of the cruciate ligament in the cervical spine.
back:
• Binds the dens of the axis to the anterior arch of the atlas
• Forms the posterior wall of the 'socket' for the dens
• Prevents posterior displacement of the dens into the spinal cord

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Distinguish between the primary and secondary curvatures of the vertebral column with respect to the cervical region.
back:
• Primary: Thoracic/Sacral (anteriorly concave), present at birth
• Secondary: Cervical (posteriorly concave/lordosis), forms when the infant begins to lift their head

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: State the hallmark anatomical features of a typical cervical vertebra (C3-C6).
back:
• Small, broad body with uncinate processes
• Bifid spinous process
• Transverse process with foramen transversarium and anterior/posterior tubercles

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: The cervical region of the adult vertebral column is composed of [___] distinct vertebrae, forming a posterior concavity known as a secondary curvature.
back:
7.
- These are numbered C1 through C7.
- They provide flexibility and support for the skull.
- The cervical curve develops as an infant begins to lift their head.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: A gymnast suffers a high-velocity injury to the neck. Imaging reveals a fracture through the ring-like first cervical vertebra which lacks a vertebral body. Name this specific vertebra.
back:
Atlas (C1).
- It lacks a body and a spinous process.
- Consists of anterior and posterior arches.
- Articulates with the occipital condyles to allow nodding movements.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Describe the functional mechanism of the odontoid process (dens) during head movement.
back:
Pivot Joint Mechanism:
- The dens projects upward from the body of C2 (Axis).
- It acts as a pivot for C1 (Atlas) to rotate.
- Facilitates the "no" (rotational) movement of the head.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Contrast the morphological features of the Atlas (C1) with those of the Vertebra Prominens (C7).
back:
C1 vs C7:
- C1: Ring-shaped; no body; no spinous process.
- C7: Large body; longest, non-bifid spinous process.
- C1: Supports skull; C7: Landmark for vertebral counting.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Identify the specific anatomical passage found in all cervical transverse processes and list its primary vascular contents.
back:
Foramen Transversarium:
- Found in C1 to C7.
- Transmits the vertebral artery (C1-C6).
- Transmits the vertebral veins (C1-C7).
- Crucial for cerebral blood supply.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Typical cervical vertebrae (C3 through C6) are distinguished from other spinal regions by the presence of [___] spinous processes.
back:
Bifid spinous processes.
- These spines are short and split into two tips.
- This feature is unique to typical cervical vertebrae.
- Allows for muscle and ligament attachments.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: While palpating a patient's neck, a clinician identifies a prominent, non-bifid bony projection at the base of the neck. Which specific vertebra serves as this clinical landmark?
back:
Seventh Cervical Vertebra (Vertebra Prominens).
- Possesses the longest spinous process in the cervical region.
- The process is thick and easily palpable.
- Foramen transversarium here is small, transmitting only veins.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Explain the role of the superior articular facets of the Atlas (C1) in the "Yes" movement of the head.
back:
Atlanto-Occipital Mechanism:
- Superior facets are concave and bean-shaped.
- They articulate with the convex occipital condyles.
- Form synovial joints allowing flexion/extension (nodding).

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Differentiate between the structural roles of the anterior and posterior arches in the C1 vertebra.
back:
C1 Arches:
- Anterior Arch: Bears a facet for the dens (C2).
- Posterior Arch: Features a groove for the vertebral artery.
- Together they form the vertebral foramen for the spinal cord.

category: Enumerate the types of cervical vertebrae and list the differences between them
front: Name the unique synovial joints found at the lateral margins of the intervertebral discs between C3 and C7.
back:
Uncovertebral Joints (Joints of Luschka):
- Found between the uncinate processes and adjacent bodies.
- Located at the lateral sides of discs.
- Common site for osteophyte formation and nerve compression.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: The distinguishing feature of all cervical vertebrae is the presence of a [___] in the transverse process.
back: Foramen transversarium. It transmits the vertebral artery (C1-C6), vertebral veins (C1-C7), and sympathetic nerve plexuses.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A victim of a high-velocity car accident presents with a bilateral fracture of the pedicles of the C2 vertebra. Identify the specific clinical name for this injury.
back: Hangman's Fracture. It results from forceful hyperextension of the head on the neck, typically fracturing the pedicles or laminae of the Axis (C2).

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Explain the role of the dens (odontoid process) and the transverse ligament of the atlas during head rotation.
back: The dens of the axis (C2) acts as a pivot. The transverse ligament of the atlas (C1) binds the dens to the anterior arch, allowing the atlas to rotate around it.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A patient presents with a 'Jefferson fracture' following a diving accident. Contrast the anatomical site of this injury with a typical 'dens fracture'.
back: Jefferson Fracture: Burst fracture of the anterior and posterior arches of the Atlas (C1). Dens Fracture: Fracture specifically involving the odontoid process of the Axis (C2).

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Describe the unique anatomical characteristics of the C7 vertebra (vertebra prominens) regarding its spine and foramen transversarium.
back: C7 has a long, non-bifid spinous process. Its foramen transversarium is small and typically transmits only the vertebral vein, not the vertebral artery.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: The first cervical vertebra (C1) is distinguished from typical vertebrae because it lacks a [___] and a spinous process.
back: Vertebral Body. C1 (Atlas) consists simply of an anterior arch, a posterior arch, and two lateral masses.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A patient presents with wasting of the small muscles of the hand (T1 distribution) and diminished radial pulse. Identify the cervical skeletal anomaly most likely causing this compression.
back: Cervical Rib. An extra rib arising from the transverse process of C7, potentially compressing the subclavian artery and the lower trunk (C8-T1) of the brachial plexus.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Explain the mechanical consequence of a rupture of the Alar ligaments during forensic neck examination.
back: Alar ligaments limit rotation of the head. Rupture leads to an increased range of rotation between the atlas and the skull, indicating severe craniovertebral trauma.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Contrast the primary movement permitted by the atlanto-occipital joints with that of the atlanto-axial joints.
back: Atlanto-occipital: 'Yes' movement (nodding/flexion-extension). Atlanto-axial: 'No' movement (rotation).

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Identify the specific features of a 'typical' cervical vertebra (C3-C6) spinous process and vertebral foramen.
back: Spinous process is short and bifid (split). Vertebral foramen is large and triangular to accommodate the cervical enlargement of the spinal cord.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: The distinguishing feature present in the transverse processes of all cervical vertebrae, facilitating the passage of the vertebral artery in C1-C6, is the [___].
back: ● Foramen transversarium. ● C1-C6 transmit the vertebral artery and plexus of sympathetic nerves. ● C7 transmits only the accessory vertebral vein.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A 19-year-old male sustains a 'Hangman’s fracture' following sudden hyperextension of the neck. This injury typically involves the pedicles of the [___] vertebra.
back: ● Axis (C2). ● Characterized by the dens (odontoid process) which acts as a pivot. ● It represents the fused body of the atlas (C1).

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Explain the role of the dens (odontoid process) in the pivot mechanism of the head.
back: ● It acts as a stationary axis for rotation. ● It articulates with the anterior arch of the atlas. ● Facilitates the 'no' movement (rotation) of the head.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Contrast the anatomical configuration of the Atlas (C1) with that of a typical cervical vertebra (C3-C6).
back: ● Atlas lacks a vertebral body and a spinous process. ● It consists of anterior/posterior arches and lateral masses. ● Typical vertebrae possess a small body and bifid spine.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Identify the prominent landmark on the C6 transverse process against which the carotid pulse can be compressed.
back: ● Carotid tubercle (Chassaignac’s tubercle). ● It is the anterior tubercle of the C6 transverse process. ● Useful clinical site for controlling carotid hemorrhage.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: The [___] is the name given to the C7 vertebra because it possesses the longest, non-bifid spinous process.
back: ● Vertebra Prominens. ● Its spine is a key surface landmark at the base of the neck. ● Foramen transversarium here is small and artery-free.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: A patient presents with limited neck flexion. Anatomy reveals a thick fibrous band connecting the external occipital protuberance to the C7 spine. This structure is the [___].
back: ● Ligamentum nuchae. ● A fibroelastic membrane representing the upward continuation of the supraspinous ligament. ● Provides attachment for trapezius and splenius capitis muscles.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: How does the transverse ligament of the atlas maintain the integrity of the atlanto-axial complex?
back: ● Arches across the ring of the atlas behind the dens. ● Holds the dens firmly against the anterior arch of C1. ● Prevents posterior displacement of the dens into the spinal cord.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Distinguish between the cervical and thoracic vertebral curvatures in terms of their developmental classification.
back: ● Cervical: Secondary curvature (anteriorly convex/posteriorly concave). ● Thoracic: Primary curvature (anteriorly concave). ● Cervical curve develops when an infant lifts its head.

category: Describe the anatomical features and attachments on cervical vertebrae
front: Enumerate three characteristic features of typical (C3-C6) cervical vertebrae.
back: ● Small, broad vertebral bodies. ● Bifid spinous processes. ● Triangular vertebral foramina and foramina transversaria in transverse processes.

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: The specialized joints found in the lower cervical spine between the uncinate processes and the adjacent vertebral bodies are known as [___].
back: Uncovertebral joints (Joints of Luschka). These are small synovial joints located at the lateral margins of the intervertebral discs from C3 to C7, often involved in osteophyte formation.

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: A patient involved in a high-velocity car accident experiences severe neck hyperextension (whiplash). Which cervical ligament is most likely to be ruptured?
back: Anterior Longitudinal Ligament (ALL). It is a strong, fibrous band that runs along the anterior surface of the vertebral bodies and specifically resists hyperextension of the spine.

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: Explain the anatomical mechanism that allows the 'No' movement (rotation) at the atlantoaxial joint.
back: The dens (odontoid process) of C2 acts as a pivot articulating with the anterior arch of the atlas. Rotation is facilitated by the transverse ligament of the atlas, which secures the dens.

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: Contrast the primary movement permitted by the atlanto-occipital joint with that of the atlantoaxial joint.
back: The atlanto-occipital joint (condylar) permits flexion and extension ('Yes' nodding). The atlantoaxial joint (pivot/plane) primarily allows rotation ('No' shaking).

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: Identify the primary muscles responsible for neck flexion and their associated nerve supply.
back: Muscles: Sternocleidomastoid, Longus colli, and Scalene muscles. Nerve Supply: Spinal Accessory nerve (CN XI) for Sternocleidomastoid; anterior rami of cervical spinal nerves for others.

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: The [___] ligament connects the odontoid process to the medial sides of the occipital condyles and serves as a 'check' to limit excessive rotation of the head.
back: Alar ligament. These paired ligaments are essential for stabilizing the craniovertebral junction and preventing excessive rotation.

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: Following a dive into a shallow pool, a patient sustains a burst fracture of the C1 ring (Jefferson fracture). This injury typically involves the rupture of [___].
back: The Transverse Ligament of the Atlas. This ligament is the primary stabilizer of the atlantoaxial joint; its rupture leads to instability of the dens relative to the atlas.

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: Describe how the Membrana Tectoria is related to the posterior longitudinal ligament.
back: The Membrana Tectoria is the upward continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament. It extends from the body of C2 to the internal surface of the occipital bone (foramen magnum).

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: Distinguish between the Ligamentum Flavum and the Ligamentum Nuchae in terms of location and function.
back: Ligamentum Flavum: Connects adjacent laminae; high elastic content helps restore upright posture. Ligamentum Nuchae: Connects spinous processes from C7 to occipital protuberance; provides muscle attachment surface.

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: Specify the primary arterial supply for the cervical vertebrae and the nerves innervating the facet (zygapophysial) joints.
back: Arterial Supply: Vertebral arteries (branches of subclavian). Nerve Supply: Medial branches of the posterior rami of cervical spinal nerves.

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
front: The [___] ligament is the upward continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament that covers the posterior surface of the dens and alar ligaments.
back:
Membrana Tectoria
* Attached above to the occipital bone within the foramen magnum.
* Provides a protective covering for the deeper odontoid ligaments.

category: Classify the joints of cervical vertebrae mentioning their ligaments, movements with muscle producing them and neurovascular supply
